text: BOGOTA -- The number of people injured in an explosive attack on the government headquarters of the Meta department in central Colombia on Monday has risen to 23, local media reported Tuesday.

The injured, who sustained injuries of varying severity, were taken to several medical facilities in Villavicencio, the capital of the Meta department. No fatalities have been reported, the report cited health authorities as saying. (Colombia-Attack)
GAZA -- Hamas internal security head and at least six other Palestinians were killed Tuesday by Israeli fire in the Gaza Strip, according to Palestinian security and medical sources.

Local sources said that Naim Abu Nahal, head of the Hamas-run internal security service, was killed after an Israeli drone fired a missile at a tent west of Gaza City, causing a large explosion in an area crowded with tents housing displaced people. (Gaza-Israeli Fire-Hamas)

PYONGYANG -- A senior official of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) said Tuesday she would advise the Foreign Ministry to consider closing the Swiss diplomatic office in Pyongyang, condemning Switzerland for imposing sanctions on a children's camp in her country, the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reported.

Kim Yo Jong, department director of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea, said in a press statement that the Swiss authorities put the Songdowon International Children's Camp of the DPRK on its sanctions list just a few days after a Swiss delegation visited Pyongyang to discuss the development of bilateral ties and pledged to pursue dialogue and cooperation. (DPRK-Switzerland-Ties)

NEW YORK -- The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on Monday imposed sanctions on over two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies and key personnel in an effort to sever Iran's global shadow banking networks.

The action, part of Operation Economic Outcast, targets the financial infrastructure that underpins much of Iran's remaining foreign trade, disrupting the exchange houses, front companies, and facilitators that move billions of dollars through the international financial system to provide Iran with access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions, the U.S. Treasury Department said in a press release. items.title: News Analysis: Belgium's education reforms fuel social discontent over austerity
text: BRUSSELS, Nov. 23 (Xinhua) -- About 50,000 people marched through Brussels on Monday in a national demonstration called by Belgium's three main trade unions against the federal government's austerity measures and declining purchasing power. Youth and civil society groups also joined the protest, reflecting growing discontent with the government's economic and social policies.

The demonstration came amid a series of student protests over education reforms, which have broadened opposition to the government's policies beyond workers and pensioners to include younger generations.

On International Students' Day on Nov. 17, about 3,200 people marched through Brussels to protest rising higher education costs and cuts to education spending. Organized by the French-speaking Students' Federation (FEF), the march brought together secondary school and university students, alongside members of the Flemish Union of Students. Belgium's two largest trade unions, the General Labor Federation of Belgium (FGTB) and the Confederation of Christian Trade Unions, also voiced support.

The march was initially peaceful but turned violent after some protesters blocked roads in the city center and clashed with police. Officers responded with water cannon and tear gas and made several arrests.

At the heart of student opposition is growing concern over the affordability of higher education. In French-speaking Belgium, changes to university tuition fees have raised fears that studying could become increasingly difficult for students from middle- and lower-income families. Although reductions and exemptions remain available to those from lower-income households, student organizations warn that higher fees could undermine equal access to education.

Low tuition fees have long been considered an important means of ensuring broad access to higher education in Belgium. The recent changes have therefore reignited debate over how education should be funded and who should bear the financial burden.

The pressure extends well beyond tuition. Housing, food, transport and study materials are also weighing heavily on student budgets. Lenaik Dumont, president of the FEF, told Xinhua in a written interview that the combined cost of education and daily living has placed increasing strain on students and their families.
"How can one claim to guarantee equal opportunities if access to studies depends more and more on one's financial means?" she said.

Concerns are also growing in Dutch-speaking Flanders, where cuts to higher education funding and changes to the student grant system have prompted criticism. Tighter eligibility requirements for financial assistance have raised fears that some students could find it harder to obtain the support they need. Although the measures differ between Belgium's language communities, both have fueled concerns about the affordability and accessibility of higher education.
Opposition to austerity has increasingly brought different social groups together.

items.title: China extends US dual-use export control suspension to 2027
text: China will extend the suspension of certain export controls on dual-use items bound for the United States from Nov 28 to Jan 27, 2027, the Ministry of Commerce said on Tuesday.

Introduced in December 2024, the measures stipulate that exports of dual-use items (goods, technologies, and services that can be used for both civilian and military purposes) related to gallium, germanium, antimony, and superhard materials to the US are "not permitted in principle".
They also require "stricter end-user and end-use reviews" for exports of dual-use graphite items to the US.
The ministry first suspended the measures on Nov 9 last year, with the suspension previously set to expire on Nov 27.

items.title: Why does China matter to Malaysia Airlines?
Intl development experts discuss urban priorities in Shanghai
text:
By Zheng Zheng in Shanghai | 
          chinadaily.com.cn |
          Updated: 2026-11-24 14:54

More than 100 government representatives, technical experts and development partners from China and 10 other countries convened in Shanghai on Monday for RISE Week 2026, a platform aimed at turning urban resilience priorities into actionable, bankable projects.

Jointly hosted by the United Nations Development Programme and Tongji University, the event brings together delegates from nations including Cambodia, Indonesia, Kenya, Malaysia, the Maldives and Sri Lanka, alongside international organizations and financial institutions, to address escalating climate and disaster risks facing cities worldwide and seek to deepen South-South cooperation by linking local urban needs with technical expertise and financing channels.

"Good technical solutions cannot stand alone," said Xu Haoliang, UN undersecretary general and UNDP associate administrator. "To make a difference on the ground, they need to fit into national and city plans and be backed by finance. South-South and triangular cooperation can help close that gap by sharing knowledge, building catalytic partnerships and mobilizing innovative financing, so that technically sound solutions become country-led, bankable investments."

Zheng Qinghua, Party secretary of Tongji University and member of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, said that jointly building resilient cities of the future embodies humanity's aspirations for a better life and a shared desire for safer, more trustworthy and more reliable places to live. This requires bringing together global expertise, breaking down disciplinary barriers, strengthening research on the use of artificial intelligence in building resilient cities, and improving the quality and efficiency of urban development.

items.title: Pakistani astronaut set to become first foreign crew member aboard Tiangong
text: China's Tiangong space station is poised to welcome its first foreign astronaut — Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who will also become the first citizen of his country to travel beyond Earth's atmosphere.

The wing commander in the Pakistan Air Force is set to fly to the orbital outpost with two Chinese astronauts — Major General Tang Hongbo, commander of the Shenzhou XXIV mission, and Colonel Wu Yi, the crew's spaceflight engineer. Their spacecraft is scheduled to lift off aboard a Long March 2F rocket at 8:18 am on Wednesday from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, Zhang Jingbo, a senior engineer and spokesman for the China Manned Space Agency, said.

At a news conference on Tuesday morning at the Jiuquan spaceport, Zhang told reporters that the rocket's propellant injection was scheduled to begin at its service tower later that day and that other prelaunch preparations were proceeding in an orderly manner.

"After the Shenzhou XXIV spacecraft enters its preset orbital position, it will activate the rapid autonomous rendezvous-docking mode and use about three and a half hours to approach and connect with the front port on the Tianhe core module," he said.

items.title: Margin finance shift fuels market surge
text: The latest move by China's securities regulator to ease margin financing rules will help improve stock market liquidity and bolster investor confidence, underscoring policymakers' readiness to respond in a timely and targeted fashion, as a sharp sell-off in overseas equities fuels renewed volatility across global markets.

With the approval of the China Securities Regulatory Commission, bourses in Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing announced on Sunday that the minimum margin requirement on securities bought with borrowed funds will be lowered from 100 percent to 80 percent, effective Nov 30. At 80 percent, 1 million yuan ($150,000) of collateral supports up to 1.25 million yuan of borrowing, raising the leverage ceiling from one-fold to 1.25-fold.

The Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges announced a new round of fee cuts worth 2.76 billion yuan and extended earlier waivers through 2028, bringing their relief for 2026 to more than 4.6 billion yuan. The Shenzhen bourse also sought public comment on draft market-making rules for the tech-heavy ChiNext, requiring continuous two-way quotes from market makers, which it said would add liquidity and improve pricing efficiency.
Dong Ximiao, chief researcher at Merchants Union Consumer Finance, said the package carries a clear signal.

The margin adjustment fits the pattern of countercyclical moves in recent years and should help the market create stable expectations that leverage tools are positioned in a normal, adjustable range, Dong said, adding that market making on the ChiNext shifts the focus of market support from external backstops toward trading infrastructure, which could improve how longer-term investors view the board's trading climate.

Dong said the effect on liquidity would build up gradually, while fee relief extended through 2028 provides participants with more cost outlook transparency, adding that he expects the capital market to maintain stable development over the long term.

The measures were met with a firm market response on Monday. The Shanghai Composite Index opened 0.86 percent lower but closed up 0.15 percent at 3,538.95 points, while the Shenzhen Component Index gained 1.93 percent and the ChiNext climbed 3.08 percent to 2,280.20. The Beijing Stock Exchange 50 index added 4.67 percent. Turnover across the three bourses reached 1.56 trillion yuan, up 132.9 billion yuan from Friday, with 4,655 shares advancing and 151 closing at the daily limit. Robot makers, film and media companies, and medical services were among the top performers.

Yang Delong, chief economist at First Seafront Fund Management, described the weekend measures as timely. Early pressure came from overseas markets, where the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28 percent and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index nearly 11 percent on Friday, a slide he said was within expectations after years of gains had pushed valuations to historic highs.

items.title: Surgeon saves overseas worker's severed thumb, 40 hours after accident
text: With nearly 1,000 finger reattachment surgeries under his belt, surgeon Wei Qingyu had never doubted the chances of success in the operating theater — until he was presented with a thumb that had been severed for 40 hours.
The case involved a worker surnamed Wang, who got injured at a construction site in Libya on Sept 7, when a steel wire rope suddenly sprang up and severed his left thumb.
Local medical institutions could not perform the replantation, so he had to return to China for treatment.

He first flew to Turkiye, then to Shanghai and from there caught another flight to Chengdu, capital of Sichuan province. At around 3 am on Sept 9, Wang finally arrived at No 1 Orthopedics Hospital of Chengdu.

"The patient's left thumb was severed at the base, with only a small amount of skin still attached. The blood vessels were completely ruptured, and the bone was fractured in two places," said Wei at the hospital's repair and reconstruction surgery department.

"The golden period for replantation is only six to eight hours. The longer the delay, the exponentially higher the risk of necrosis in blood vessels, nerves and muscles," he said, adding that a 40-hour post-detachment period presented challenges.
Such a lengthy period is rare in replantation cases both at home and abroad. According to Wei, the longest case the hospital had previously handled was under 30 hours.
Despite nearly nine years of experience in replantation surgery, handling more than 100 cases a year, Wei admitted he could not guarantee success in Wang's case.
"In fact, the patient also had little confidence in replantation himself," Wei said. "He told us that he came to the hospital prepared for thumb reconstruction."
Thumb reconstruction refers to building a new thumb using materials from elsewhere on the body, such as skin, nail and joints from a toe.
"The original thumb is always the best. So after discussing it with the patient, we decided to try replantation first, and turn to reconstruction if it failed," Wei said.

Upon Wang's admission, the hospital immediately opened a green channel for emergency treatment. The medical team from the repair and reconstruction surgery department sprinted into action, while the anesthesia and operating center units simultaneously made preparations, ensuring a seamless treatment process.
"Even beyond the golden period for replantation, as long as there is a glimmer of hope, we will not easily give up," said Zhou Mengsen, director of the department.

Replantation requires surgeons to work under a microscope, reattaching blood vessels and nerves so fine that some are thinner than a strand of human hair, along with tendons and bone. Wang's case was even more challenging, as the prolonged detachment had caused severe necrosis in the severed thumb's blood vessels, according to the medical team.
The operation, which lasted nearly three hours, was a success.
"Normally, once the artery is reconnected, the thumb would regain color within two or three seconds. In this case, it took about half a minute before blood flow gradually resumed," Wei said.

items.title: A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019309/A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
text: “Xiao Ming and his mom and dad are eating out at a restaurant. After they finish eating, his mom wants to take home the leftovers, but his dad thinks it’s unbecoming. What would you do and say if you were Xiao Ming?” poses a Chinese exam question.
“If I were Xiao Ming, I would tell my mom not to pack the leftovers because we have plenty of money, and it would be embarrassing if people saw us doing so,” one student responds.

This answer to a primary school Chinese language exam question has sparked online debate over how schools should balance encouraging children to express their opinions with promoting moral values, with a related hashtag attracting over 46 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

The controversy began when the parent of a third-grader in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, shared a photo of the assignment alongside their child’s answer in a WeChat parent group, which was later leaked, according to domestic media. The child’s teacher marked the answer incorrect, deducting all four potential points. Above, a large red check mark adorns a revised answer written by the student that states: “1) I would pack the leftovers with my family. 2) I would tell my dad that all food is grown through the hard work of farmers, and we shouldn’t waste it just because we’re afraid of losing face.”

Many social media users pointed out the apparent conflict between nurturing critical thinking and penalizing it. “It’s unreasonable to punish students for such answers in a Chinese language exam,” one user wrote. “While it may appear to promote ‘the right values,’ deducting scores as a means of enforcement only teaches children to lie to get what they want.”

Others agreed with the teacher, saying that schools also have a responsibility to help children develop sound values and moral judgment. “(Children) should be encouraged to think outside the box, but their ideas must be grounded in the correct values,” wrote another user.

In recent years, China has sought to curb food waste, enacting the Anti-Food Waste Law in 2021 to cut waste across the food supply chain. In 2020, the Ministry of Education also urged schools to teach frugality and the importance of reducing leftovers. Authorities have also cracked down in recent years on banquets, discouraging excessive food ordering as a display of wealth and generosity.

Zhao Tongwei, a senior teacher and principal of Shanghai-based Shengqiao Central Primary School, told local media that the student’s response reflected a tension between attitudes absorbed from everyday life and the values schools seek to promote.
“Chinese language education is about more than teaching practical skills; it also has a humanistic and educational role. Upholding sound values is a principle that must not be compromised,” he said.

The aim, Zhao said, should be to help students think for themselves. Simply deducting marks could discourage children from expressing what they genuinely believe, he warned, and instead advocate reflection through writing exercises, one-on-one conversations, or whole-class discussions on the topic.
(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

items.title: Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019315/Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
text: Almost 30 years ago, Carrie Bradshaw opened the TV phenomenon “Sex and the City” with a question: “Why are there so many great unmarried women, and no great unmarried men?” Later, she backs up her assertion with data, declaring that “there are 1.3 million single men in New York, (and) 1.8 million single women.”

Carrie was speaking about turn-of-the-millennium New York, but women in major Chinese cities such as Beijing and Shanghai will have little problem understanding her plight. Marriage rates have declined across the board in recent years, but the drop has been felt most keenly by two very different groups: urban women and rural men.

To get an idea of the problem, take a map of China and color each prefecture-level city red if men there are more likely to be single than women, and blue if the reverse is true. The result is striking. Less developed inland provinces such as Yunnan, Guizhou, and Gansu turn deep red. The country’s richest urban clusters — the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta, and the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region — turn deep blue. The line between them follows, almost exactly, the line between China’s poorer and wealthier regions.
In other words, China’s cities are full of highly educated single women. In less developed areas, singles are disproportionately men with little education.

China’s skewed sex ratio can explain why there are more single men than single women overall. Yet it cannot fully explain the geographic distribution of single men and women. For its part, media coverage tends to oversimplify the phenomenon as a problem of willingness, with young Chinese rejecting the concept of marriage altogether.

But is that true? Our research, based on two decades of data from national population censuses and the comprehensive China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) surveys, paints a more complete — and complex — picture of how demographic transformation in educational attainment, regional imbalances in skills and industries, and cultural norms have contributed to China’s unbalanced marriage market.

Let’s start with education. Over the past several decades, Chinese women have quietly but quickly caught up with men in educational attainment. Among Chinese born between 1960 and 1995, the education gap between men and women steadily narrowed. For the cohort born around 1985, women college graduates outnumber their male counterparts. And for Chinese born in the mid-1990s or later, the gap in women’s favor is large and continues to widen, especially at the postgraduate level.

This shift coincided with a decisive transformation in China’s economic structure. The services sector, which is disproportionately concentrated in major cities, has grown, drawing women, especially those with degrees, out of agriculture and manufacturing. In 2000, college-educated women were 17 percentage points less likely than college-educated men to work in the services sector; by 2015, they were 21 points more likely to hold such positions.

items.title: Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019305/Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
text: Chinese archaeologists have announced discoveries from four sites across the country, including Paleolithic campsite ruins and greater details of an aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture.

The findings, announced at a Wednesday conference held by China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration, come from four years of work at four sites along the Yangtze River. They include Taohuahe in the southwestern Sichuan province; Fanshan in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province; Lingtoushang in the eastern Jiangxi province; and Laohudun in the central Hubei province.
The discoveries were presented by Archaeology China, a government program launched in 2018 to fund long-term excavations investigating the origins of farming and civilization.

Taohuahe, discovered in 2022, has yielded over 13,000 Paleolithic-age stone artifacts, including large stone choppers, and 179 animal fossils dating from 300,000 to 50,000 years ago, researchers at the conference announced. Excavations have also revealed stone-working and storage areas, cobblestone surfaces, and a semicircular refuse pit.
Wang Youping, an archaeologist at Peking University, told domestic media that, unlike in other archaeological digs in southern China, numerous animal bones have been recovered at Taohuahe.

“Southern China’s acidic soil usually destroys bone,” Wang said. “Researchers had assumed that people in the lush south relied mainly on plants. The (presence of animal) bones suggests that meat was equally important to their work, daily lives, and evolution.”

The second site discussed at the meeting, Fanshan, was discovered 40 years ago and is the highest-ranking aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture ever found, researchers said. The Liangzhu culture, located in northern present-day Hangzhou, flourished about 5,000 years ago. UNESCO added the ruins of its walled city and system of dams and reservoirs to its World Heritage List in 2019.

Excavations that began in 2024 indicate that a walled compound enclosed the site’s cemetery mound. At least three buildings stood at its center, including a large oval structure raised on stilts, likely used for ceremonies. The compound lies on a ridge that formed part of the surrounding area’s water system, leading researchers to hypothesize that the tombs, ritual spaces, and dams were planned as a single complex.

After last year’s discovery of a courtyard wall at the Fanshan site, archaeologists uncovered a group of three related buildings this year. Wang said the wall may have formed the cemetery’s outer boundary, while the buildings may have served as sacrificial halls. He added that the culture may already have had a mausoleum system.

Researchers also announced at the conference that they have discovered Neolithic and Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) settlements at a third site, Lingtoushang. The settlements contained evidence of smelting and large quantities of copper, shedding light on close cultural exchange and how the societies exploited and controlled metal resources.

items.title: Lost Ground: China’s Coffee Brands Break Starbucks and Nestlé’s Grip on Yunnan
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019307/Lost Ground: China’s Coffee Brands Break Starbucks and Nestlé’s Grip on Yunnan
text: For coffee growers in China’s southwestern Yunnan province, Starbucks and Nestlé used to be the only buyers in town. Every harvest season, their purchasing stations would have lines of loaded trucks stretching for days.

Plantation owner Zou Qingquan recalls once waiting a whole week to sell her beans to Nestlé. Back then, she says, the company revised its purchase price twice a week based on changes in the international commodity market, “so your beans were making or losing money as they sat there in the truck.”

Over the past five years, however, these two global giants have been losing their grip on the Yunnan coffee market. Rapid growth among domestic brands such as Seesaw, Manner, Luckin, and the Mixue Group, along with a shift toward specialty coffee, has opened new sales channels for farmers and pushed up prices.

According to the agricultural industry analysis platform Beedata, Nestlé and Starbucks paid an average of 48.09 yuan ($7.20) and 48.18 yuan per kilogram, respectively, for commercial-grade Yunnan green beans in the first quarter of 2026. For Luckin, it was 50.37 yuan.

But while growers’ incomes have risen, some warn that an increasingly indiscriminate buying frenzy, which in some cases is leading to the sale of unripe beans, risks disrupting established trade relationships and negatively affecting the quality and image of Yunnan coffee.

Ma Xiaojin, who manages two coffee-growing cooperatives in Yunnan’s Menglian Dai, Lahu and Va Autonomous County, used to regularly drive the 10 hours from his farm to the Starbucks Farmer Support Center, a training and purchasing facility in central Pu’er, a city arguably best known for its eponymous tea. There, he’d join the line of trucks and wait four or five days to have his beans graded, costing him at least 2,000 yuan in truck rental costs.

Starbucks has exacting quality standards and purchases beans only from growers certified under its Coffee and Farmer Equity (CAFE) Practices program, which in January included 3,400 farms in Yunnan. The American company is also known for paying more for high-quality beans than its Swiss competitor, Nestlé.

“You can’t just show up and expect Starbucks to take your beans,” says Hao Yi, who used to work for Starbucks in coffee production. “They don’t just check each batch; they monitor your quality over several consecutive years. That’s why, in the early days, getting your beans into Starbucks was a source of pride. It also brought your subsequent harvests to the attention of specialty coffee roasters.”

In 2017, Starbucks began selling selected Yunnan beans as part of its high-end Reserve line. For growers, making the cut was no easy feat. If their products passed a preliminary check, they had to provide three large samples from each sack for testing and agree to follow-up screenings.

Specialty beans from Zou’s estate were selected in 2021, with Starbucks offering 48 yuan per kilogram. At the time, her farm was selling to the open market for more than 60 yuan per kilogram. “We earned less, but working with a big brand was good publicity for us, so it was still a net gain,” she says. The following year, many new buyers approached Zou to purchase the same beans.

items.title: China sets new record in deep oil well casing replacement in Xinjiang region
text: The Xinjiang Oilfield, a major oil production base in northwestern China, belonging to the China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) has announced that it has completed a deep underground casing replacement trial at a depth of 1,819 meters, setting a new domestic record and marking progress in technologies designed to repair aging oil wells and extend their service life, the China News Service reported Saturday.

The expanded field trial was recently completed at a Gobi Desert drilling site in the Luliang oilfield, with the operation successfully reconnecting 1,819 meters of casing and completing cementing work in the space between the casing and the surrounding wellbore.

The achievement extends the limits of a technique developed by the oilfield to tackle severe damage to underground well casings, which can otherwise make wells difficult to maintain and continue operating.

In an oil well, steel casing pipes are installed inside the drill hole to support the well walls and provide a stable passage for extracting oil or injecting water. Over years of operation, however, these pipes can corrode, become deformed or break, potentially restricting the well's internal passage and disrupting production.

At the Xinjiang Oilfield, located in the Junggar Basin in Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, prolonged exposure to highly mineralized water and the gradual deformation of water-absorbing mudstone formations have contributed to increasingly serious casing damage, including large sections suffering leakage and broken pipes.

Conventional repair methods, such as plugging damaged sections, may only address the immediate leakage without removing the underlying damaged casing. Meanwhile, traditional casing replacement techniques used in shallower sections are not well suited to the complicated conditions encountered deeper underground.

To address the problem, researchers at the Xinjiang Oilfield's Oil Production Technology Research Institute developed a deep open-hole casing replacement technique in 2025. The approach involves removing damaged casing sections and installing replacement pipes, aiming to restore the wellbore to its original internal diameter rather than simply sealing the damaged areas.

An initial field trial was successfully conducted in October 2025 at Well 1424, operated by the Baikouquan Oil Production Plant. The operation replaced casings at a depth of 996 meters and accomplished 809 meters of open-hole casing milling, setting two domestic records at the time.
Building on the experience, the research team continued refining the technique in 2026, focusing on several challenges that had affected the efficiency and safety of deep underground operations.

These included difficulties in milling long unsupported sections of casing, the risk of tools becoming stuck when working along the edge of the casing, and the time-consuming process of cutting and retrieving damaged pipes at greater depths.

Congress to grill Jensen Huang over ties with China and Trump’s intervention
text: Lawmakers from both parties outraged over Nvidia CEO’s reinstatement and the administration’s handling of national security risks

Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s chief executive is “exhibit A” of the “political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration’s big tech and AI policy”, Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat vying to become the next Senate majority leader, told reporters Monday.

Van Hollen said he intends to focus on Huang’s “efforts to increase and accelerate the export of high-end chips to China, how he’s been accomplishing that, how he’s been getting his way with the administration” when the reinstalled Nvidia CEO appears before the Senate banking committee on 3 December.

It will be one of several appearances on Capitol Hill next week where skeptical lawmakers from both parties will grill Huang over his ties to a woman that some in the intelligence community have said was a spy for China. Huang will also sit for transcribed interviews with the House foreign affairs committee, as well as the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee.

“It’s completely hypocritical for the Trump administration, on the one hand, to say the reason we have to take all the brakes off AI development here at home is because China will leap ahead if we don’t,” Van Hollen said. “When in fact, it’s the Trump administration that’s helping China leap ahead.”

Nvidia’s board reinstated Huang after Donald Trump intervened on the executive’s behalf, assuring company leadership that he did not pose a national security risk despite questions surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, a tech executive of no relation who has been accused of acting as a Chinese asset and routing advanced chips to Beijing via her data center company, Megaspeed.

In an interview with CNBC on Monday, the US president defended his involvement in Huang’s reinstatement, arguing it would be a “bigger threat” for Nvidia to lose Huang’s “brain power” in the AI race. Trump also confirmed that he had provided the board with assurances regarding any national security concerns.
“I spoke to them, let me put it that way. And I convinced them,” Trump said.

Van Hollen pointed to a series of ties between Huang and Trumpworld as evidence of the executive’s influence over administration policy on advanced chips, including Nvidia’s $25m donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project, his personal holdings of Nvidia stock, Huang’s contribution to Trump’s inauguration fund and his attendance at a $1m-a-plate dinner at Mar-a-Lago.

The outrage spread on Capitol Hill on Monday. Gregory Meeks, a Democrat congressman from New York and the ranking member on the foreign affairs committee, called the decision “yet another example” of how “the wealthy and well connected are held to a different standard”.

            The Communist Party chief of Shanghai, considered one of the potential heirs to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, has suddenly been placed under investigation –– marking an escalation of an anti-corruption purge that’s already ensnared a large swath of the country’s top talent.

Chen Jining, 62, who has run China’s largest city and financial center since October 2022, is facing a corruption charge and is suspected of “serious violations of discipline,” state media Xinhua said on Tuesday evening.
It is a stunning downfall for Chen, who was seen as a rising political star and even being mentioned among potential successors to longtime leader Xi by China watchers.

Xi, who is all but certain to assume a precedent-breaking fourth term in office next year, has executed an unrelenting anti-corruption drive for well over a decade that has brought down senior political, military and judiciary figures once thought untouchable. The speed and scale that effort has reached unseen levels in recent months.
Chen becomes the fourth of the 24 member politburo –– the top-echelon of power in China –– to fall since the last party congress in 2022.
The investigation is being conducted by China’s main anti-corruption body, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection.
Chen’s last public appearance appears to be Thursday, November 19, when he inspected the headquarters of a Chinese shipping conglomerate.
Unsurprisingly, government platforms in Shanghai have quickly taken down posts mentioning Chen.

China sentences official to death for spying for foreign country
text: Accused official leaked national secrets to unnamed country and received payments worth over $150,000, state-linked publisher says
A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying for a foreign country, a government-linked publisher has said.

Gold Wall Press, a publishing company associated with China’s national administration of state secrets protection, said the convicted person was surnamed Ma and was approached and recruited by an unnamed foreign intelligence service while working abroad.

Chinese courts typically do not publish information about state security cases, but in recent years the powerful ministry of state security and Gold Wall Press have increasingly publicised arrests, as well as using social media, movies and comics to promote warnings about espionage.

The statement on Monday said Ma had signed a cooperation agreement containing clauses on “confidentiality” and “loyalty” and received fixed monthly payments. In total, it said, he provided 35 pieces of information that were classified as national secrets and received payments worth more than 1m yuan ($150,000).

An intelligence operative identified as Kailin “frequently arranged to meet with Ma, hoping to engage with him more”, citing an interest in learning Chinese, the statement said. Kailin later introduced him to a colleague who threatened to report his earlier disclosures to Chinese authorities if he refused to cooperate.

After returning to China, Ma continued to gather intelligence for the foreign agency, which provided him with a laptop, the statement said. He used his position to collect material from classified documents during the day and transmitted it overseas at night via an espionage website.
The statement did not identify the countries involved, or say when or where he was sentenced or whether he had already been executed.
The case comes as US intelligence has been publicising its own efforts to recruit sources in China. The five most-viewed videos on the CIA’s YouTube channel are recruiting advertisements in Mandarin.

“This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call,” the Gold Wall Press said, warning that foreign intelligence agencies were “cunning” and used emotional ties, financial interests and threats to recruit people in key positions.
The statement also urged officials to remain vigilant, strengthen their loyalty to the Communist party, protect state secrets and guard against foreign recruitment.

In 2023 Beijing broadened its anti-espionage law, expanding the definition of espionage and strengthening the investigative powers of state security authorities. The following year it revised its state secrets law to extend restrictions on sensitive information to so-called “work secrets”.
